issues.description: The problem statement and UML describe acceptSupplyDelivery as taking four parameters (supplier name, ingredient name, price, quantity), but both the provided Main example and the solution implementation use a three-parameter signature (ingredient name, price, quantity). This mismatch will confuse students about the correct method signature to implement and which parameters are required.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the specification and examples: either (A) update the problem statement and UML to declare acceptSupplyDelivery(String ingredientName, int price, int quantity) (removing the supplier parameter), or (B) update the Main example and reference solution to implement and use acceptSupplyDelivery(String supplierName, String ingredientName, int price, int quantity). Ensure the template, examples, UML, and tests all use the same signature.

issues.description: The problem statement specifies SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery with four parameters (supplier name, ingredient name, price, quantity) — signature shown as acceptSupplyDelivery(String, String, int, int) — but both the template usage (Main.java) and the solution implement and call a three-argument version acceptSupplyDelivery(String name, int price, int quantity) that lacks the supplier-name parameter. This signature mismatch (and the missing parameter name) creates a conceptual mapping barrier: students reading the problem will expect to implement/use a 4-argument method while the provided code and reference solution use a 3-argument method.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signature consistent across artifacts. Either (A) update the problem statement to require acceptSupplyDelivery(String ingredientName, int price, int quantity) (remove the supplier parameter from the specification), or (B) update the template and solution to implement and call acceptSupplyDelivery(String supplierName, String ingredientName, int price, int quantity) and adjust all call sites (e.g., Main.java) accordingly. Ensure parameter names in the UML, description, and code match so students can map requirements to implementation unambiguously.
